overview: Newmont Corporation is the world's largest gold mining company by production and market capitalization, with a portfolio of roughly a dozen Tier 1 operating mines across the Americas, Australia, Africa, and Papua New Guinea following its November 2023 acquisition of Newcrest Mining. The company produces approximately 5.3-6 million ounces of gold annually alongside meaningful by-product copper, silver, lead, and zinc production (notably from Peñasquito and Cadia), and has spent 2024-2026 divesting non-core assets to concentrate capital on its highest-return Tier 1 and Tier 2 mines. Headquartered in Denver, Colorado, and founded in 1916, Newmont is the only gold miner in the S&P 500.

business_model.summary: Newmont makes money by mining and selling gold (and by-product copper, silver, lead, and zinc) at prevailing spot/contract commodity prices, with revenue and margins highly leveraged to the gold price. Revenue is transactional/commodity-based rather than recurring, though high-quality, long-lived, low-cost Tier 1 assets (Boddington, Tanami, Cadia, Ahafo, Peñasquito, Lihir, Cerro Negro, Merian) provide multi-decade production visibility. FY2025 revenue was $22.7B (up from $18.7B in FY2024), driven mostly by a surging realized gold price (~$4,414/oz in Q2 2026) rather than higher volumes; AISC of ~$1,621-1,680/oz means margins expand disproportionately as gold prices rise. The portfolio-optimization divestiture program (Akyem, CC&V, Éléonore, Porcupine, Musselwhite, Telfer, and a Canadian development project) raised approximately $4.3 billion and was substantially completed through 2025-2026, shifting the revenue base toward fewer, larger, lower-cost mines.
business_model.customer_type: B2B — gold and by-products sold into global commodity markets/refiners/traders at prevailing spot or contractual prices; no meaningful retail/consumer exposure
business_model.geographic_mix: Operations across North America (US, Mexico, Canada), South America (Argentina, Peru, Suriname), Australia, Africa (Ghana), and Papua New Guinea/Pacific (Lihir); post-Newcrest the portfolio is more geographically diversified but also more exposed to higher-risk jurisdictions (PNG, Ghana, Suriname, Mexico) than historically

competitive_position.market_position: Largest gold producer in the world by volume (~5.3-6 Moz/year) and by market capitalization (~$128-134B as of Q3 2026), roughly double Agnico Eagle's production and well ahead of Barrick. Industry-leading reserve base of ~118-134 million ounces of gold reserves plus ~149 Moz of resources, giving Newmont one of the longest reserve lives in the sector. The only gold miner in the S&P 500, which supports passive-fund ownership and liquidity.

moat_factors.description: Largest gold reserve/resource base in the industry (~118 Moz reserves), supporting decades of visible production and giving Newmont unmatched optionality to sequence its highest-return ounces first.

moat_factors.factor: Tier 1 asset quality and cost position
moat_factors.description: Portfolio concentrated (post-divestiture) in large, long-life, lower-cost mines (Boddington, Tanami, Cadia, Ahafo, Peñasquito, Lihir) generating meaningful by-product credits (copper, silver, lead, zinc) that structurally lower all-in sustaining costs versus single-metal gold-only peers.

Operating in ~8-10 countries reduces single-country/single-asset risk (e.g., the April 2026 Cadia earthquake did not derail company-wide guidance), but this cuts both ways versus Agnico Eagle's ~95% top-tier-jurisdiction concentration, which carries materially lower political risk per ounce.

Record free cash flow (Q2 2026 FCF of $2.2B) at current gold prices has funded an enhanced capital allocation framework, a new $6B buyback authorization (on top of the original program; cumulative buybacks have retired >100 million shares, ~9% of shares outstanding), and a sustainable ~$1.1B/year dividend, all while reducing net debt.
Sole S&P 500 gold miner, giving it structural demand from index funds and ETFs (e.g., GDX weighting) that smaller peers lack.

weaknesses: No pricing power — Newmont is a price-taker on gold and by-product metals, with margins entirely a function of spot prices and its own cost control

Geographically scattered, higher-risk footprint versus top peers: operations in PNG, Ghana, Suriname, Mexico, and Argentina carry materially more political, permitting, and labor risk than Agnico Eagle's largely Canada/Finland/Mexico base
Integration risk from the large, complex Newcrest acquisition still working through the system (divestiture completion, cost synergy capture, combined systems)
History of labor disputes (e.g., the 2023 three-month Peñasquito strike) and operational disruptions (April 2026 Cadia earthquake) that can take mines offline for months
Large absolute capital spending requirements (sustaining + development capex, including Tanami Expansion 2 and Cadia Panel Caves) that compete with capital-return priorities

growth_drivers: Gold price tailwind: record and near-record gold prices (intraday high near $5,590/oz in January 2026, averaging well above $4,300/oz through much of 2026) are driving outsized revenue, margin, and free cash flow growth largely independent of volume growth

Completion of the post-Newcrest portfolio optimization/divestiture program (~$4.3B raised from Akyem, CC&V, Éléonore, Porcupine, Musselwhite, Telfer and a Canadian development project), concentrating capital and management attention on fewer, higher-return Tier 1 assets

Development/expansion projects at existing assets: Tanami Expansion 2 and the Cadia Panel Caves, plus mine-life extension investments at Lihir and Cerro Negro, support medium-term production and reserve replacement without new greenfield/M&A risk

Enhanced capital allocation framework (announced February 2026) designed to systematically shrink the share count through buybacks (new $6B authorization, >100 million shares/~9% already retired) while growing the per-share dividend — a deliberate pivot toward per-share metrics rather than absolute production growth

By-product credits (copper at Cadia/Boddington, silver/lead/zinc at Peñasquito) benefiting from broader strength in base and precious metals markets, improving consolidated AISC and effectively subsidizing gold production costs
Exploration and brownfield reserve replacement across the enlarged, higher-quality post-Newcrest portfolio, supported by one of the industry's largest reserve/resource bases

business.description: The April 2026 magnitude-4.5 earthquake near Cadia idled underground mining for months (full recovery not expected before Q3 2026), illustrating how a single-site event at a large contributor can impair production and cash flow even when company-wide guidance is maintained.

business.risk: Reserve depletion and need for continuous reserve replacement
business.description: As a depleting-asset business, Newmont must continuously replace mined ounces through exploration, brownfield expansion, or acquisition to sustain production; failure to do so erodes long-term asset value even if near-term financials look strong.

History of material labor disputes, including the 2023 three-month strike at Peñasquito that halted a major silver/lead/zinc/gold operation; collective bargaining agreements across multiple countries (Mexico, Suriname, others) create recurring renewal risk.

The 2023 all-stock Newcrest combination (~$13.5-16.8B) was transformative in scale; realizing synergies, integrating systems/culture, and successfully executing the divestiture program carries ongoing execution risk even as the program nears completion.

financial.description: Revenue, margins, and free cash flow are almost entirely a function of the spot gold price (and copper/silver/lead/zinc by-product prices); a reversal of the 2024-2026 gold bull market (e.g., Goldman Sachs' lowered end-2026 forecast of $4,900/oz amid a more hawkish Fed) would compress margins sharply given largely fixed-cost mine operations.

Operating costs are incurred in multiple local currencies (AUD, PGK, GHS, SRD, MXN, ARS, CAD) while revenue is USD-denominated gold sales, creating a cost-side FX mismatch that can inflate AISC when the dollar weakens against operating-country currencies.

Large, simultaneous commitments to sustaining capex, growth capex (Tanami Expansion 2, Cadia Panel Caves), dividends (~$1.1B/year), and an aggressive $6B buyback authorization require continued strong free cash flow; a gold price pullback would force the company to prioritize among these uses.

regulatory.risk: Permitting and environmental/ESG compliance across multiple jurisdictions
regulatory.description: Operations in Ghana, Papua New Guinea, Suriname, Mexico, Peru, and Argentina each carry distinct, evolving permitting, environmental, tailings-management, and indigenous/community-relations regimes; adverse permitting decisions or new environmental regulation can delay projects or increase costs.

Suriname's tightened residence-permit requirements for foreign workers (effective Q4 2025) illustrate how sudden regulatory shifts in operating countries can raise compliance costs or staffing risk at specific mines (e.g., Merian).

Host governments across Newmont's footprint have periodically sought higher royalties, windfall taxes, or renegotiated terms amid elevated gold prices, a recurring risk for miners operating in resource-nationalist environments.

macro.description: Gold is a non-yielding asset; a more hawkish Fed path (rate cuts delayed into 2027, as flagged by Goldman Sachs in mid-2026) raises the opportunity cost of holding gold and has already driven pullbacks (e.g., gold falling below $4,350/oz and NEM shares dropping ~4.45% on September 28, 2026, on hawkish Fed signals).

Much of the 2024-2026 gold rally has been driven by record central bank buying (~289 tonnes in Q2 2026) and geopolitical/safe-haven demand; a de-escalation of geopolitical tensions or slowdown in central bank accumulation could remove a key price support.
Diesel, explosives, steel, labor, and energy costs for open-pit and underground mining are subject to broader commodity and wage inflation, pressuring AISC independent of the gold price itself.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Gold entered a structural bull cycle through 2024-2026, with prices reaching an intraday record near $5,590/oz in January 2026 before correcting to the $4,300-4,400/oz range by September 2026 amid hawkish Fed repricing. Forecasts for the remainder of 2026 and 2027 diverge widely (Goldman Sachs ~$4,900/oz by year-end 2026 on a delayed-cuts view; BNP Paribas as high as $6,000/oz; ING averaging ~$4,325/oz), reflecting genuine uncertainty about the durability of record central bank buying (averaging ~70 tonnes/month in 2026, roughly 4x the pre-2022 pace) and safe-haven/ETF demand.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Highly cyclical and commodity-price-driven; Newmont's earnings and cash flow swing dramatically with the gold price given largely fixed per-ounce mining costs, though the post-Newcrest, post-divestiture portfolio of lower-cost Tier 1 mines provides somewhat more resilience through a downturn than higher-cost peers.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and inverse — gold (and by extension Newmont's revenue) tends to benefit from falling real rates and a dovish Fed, and is vulnerable to hawkish repricing, as demonstrated by the September 28, 2026 selloff when hawkish Fed signals pushed gold below $4,350/oz and NEM shares down ~4.45% in a single session.

recent_developments.event: NEM shares fell approximately 4.45% as gold dropped below $4,350/oz on hawkish Federal Reserve signals, rising Treasury yields, and inflation concerns pressuring non-yielding assets; illustrates the stock's high beta to gold price swings.

Multiple Newmont executives (CEO Natascha Viljoen, EVP Peter Toth, EVP Peter Wexler, Group Head of Projects & Studies David Fry) sold shares in routine/planned transactions during September 2026; no insider buying reported in the trailing three months.
Newmont announced it will report Q3 2026 results after markets close on October 22, 2026; consensus EPS estimate of approximately $2.18.

Q2 2026 results reported: net income of $2.2B ($2.06/diluted share), adjusted EPS of $2.10 (up 46.9% YoY from $1.43), adjusted EBITDA of $3.8B, record free cash flow of $2.2B on operating cash flow of $2.9B. Gold sales realized at an average price of $4,414/oz; gold AISC of $1,621/oz, below the full-year guide of $1,680/oz. Returned $1.9B to shareholders via dividends and buybacks in the quarter; cumulative buybacks surpassed 100 million shares retired since program inception.

A magnitude-4.5 earthquake struck near the Cadia mine in New South Wales, Australia (the region's largest on record), triggering safety protocols and halting underground mining for an extended period; Newmont guided to 80% capacity recovery within roughly five weeks but did not expect full capacity restoration until at least Q3 2026. No injuries were reported. Despite the disruption, Newmont maintained full-year 2026 guidance, supported by processing surface stockpiles and higher output from other assets (Boddington, Tanami, Lihir, Cerro Negro, Peñasquito) weighted to H2 2026.

Newmont reaffirmed 2026 guidance alongside the Cadia disruption and announced a new $6.0 billion share repurchase authorization under its enhanced capital allocation framework (with ~$4.3B remaining under the prior authorization at the time of filing).

Newmont reported FY2025 results (revenue $22.67B, net income $7.17B) and introduced an 'Enhanced Capital Allocation Framework' explicitly targeting per-share metrics — using buybacks to permanently shrink the share count in order to drive sustainable per-share dividend growth rather than targeting absolute production growth. Management indicated the next dividend review could raise the quarterly payout toward $0.27/share, an ~8% increase since the framework's February 2026 introduction.

Newmont substantially completed its post-Newcrest divestiture program of non-core assets (Akyem, CC&V, Éléonore, Porcupine, Musselwhite, Telfer, and a Canadian development project), raising approximately $4.3 billion including contingent payments — well above the original $2 billion target — used to pay down acquisition-related debt and strengthen the balance sheet.

guidance.as_of: Q2 2026 Earnings (July 23, 2026) and FY2025/Q4 2025 guidance update (February 2026)

items.vs_prior: maintained despite the Q2 2026 Cadia earthquake disruption
items.notes: Production is guided approximately 52% weighted to H2 2026, driven by higher output at Boddington, Tanami, Lihir, Cerro Negro, and Peñasquito, with Cadia, Ahafo South, and Merian benefiting from higher grades later in the year.
Q2 2026 actual AISC of $1,621/oz came in below the full-year guide, aided by strong by-product (copper, silver, lead, zinc) credits.
Primarily funding Tanami Expansion 2, the Cadia Panel Caves, and mine-life extension investments at Lihir and Cerro Negro.

items.vs_prior: raised — enhanced capital allocation framework targets further per-share dividend growth (next review could lift quarterly payout toward $0.27/share, an ~8% increase since February 2026)
items.notes: Dividend is structured to grow on a per-share basis via share-count reduction (buybacks) rather than increasing total cash commitment.

items.target: $6.0 billion new authorization (on top of prior program)
items.vs_prior: raised/new — additional to the original buyback program
items.notes: Cumulative buybacks have retired over 100 million shares (~9% of shares outstanding) since program inception; ~$4.3B remained under the prior authorization at the time the new $6B program was announced.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO Natascha Viljoen) reiterated that Newmont remains 'on track to achieve full year guidance' despite the Cadia earthquake disruption, citing the benefit of portfolio diversification across its Tier 1 asset base. The enhanced capital allocation framework, introduced in February 2026, was explicitly framed around maximizing total shareholder return 'through the commodity and investment cycles,' prioritizing a resilient balance sheet and per-share value creation (via buyback-driven share-count reduction) over absolute production growth targets.

bull_case: Direct, high-torque exposure to a structural gold bull market: record central bank buying (~70 tonnes/month in 2026, ~4x pre-2022 levels), geopolitical/safe-haven demand, and a possible dovish Fed pivot could sustain gold well above Newmont's ~$1,680/oz AISC, driving outsized free cash flow growth

Largest, most diversified Tier 1 gold portfolio in the industry post-Newcrest, with industry-leading reserves (~118+ Moz) providing multi-decade production visibility and optionality to high-grade or defer lower-return ounces as prices fluctuate

Disciplined post-merger capital allocation: completed ~$4.3B non-core divestiture program strengthened the balance sheet, while the new enhanced framework (an additional $6B buyback authorization, >100M shares/~9% already retired, growing per-share dividend) is a credible, shareholder-friendly use of record free cash flow ($2.2B FCF in Q2 2026 alone)

Operational resilience demonstrated in 2026: despite a significant earthquake disruption at Cadia, company-wide full-year guidance was maintained, underscoring the diversification benefit of having a dozen large operating mines rather than concentrated single-asset exposure
Sole S&P 500 gold miner, generating structural passive-fund demand and liquidity advantages versus smaller peers, alongside a sector-leading production scale (~2x Agnico Eagle's output)
bear_case: Pure commodity-price dependency with no pricing power: a hawkish Fed repricing (rate cuts delayed to 2027, as flagged by Goldman Sachs) or resolution of the geopolitical/macro tensions fueling 2024-2026 safe-haven demand could trigger a sharp gold price correction, compressing margins given largely fixed per-ounce mining costs — already visible in the ~22% drawdown from January 2026's ~$5,590/oz record to the ~$4,300-4,400/oz range by September 2026, and the ~4.45% single-day share drop on September 28, 2026

Scattered, higher-risk jurisdictional footprint versus top-tier peers (PNG, Ghana, Suriname, Mexico, Argentina) exposes Newmont to recurring operational shocks — the April 2026 Cadia earthquake (idling underground mining for months) and the 2023 three-month Peñasquito strike illustrate how single-asset disruptions can materially affect company results despite overall diversification

Newcrest integration and divestiture execution, while largely complete, carried multi-year complexity and distraction risk; residual integration costs, retained-asset underperformance, or synergy shortfalls are difficult for outside investors to fully verify

Heavy and simultaneous capital commitments — sustaining capex, ~$1.4B development capex (Tanami Expansion 2, Cadia Panel Caves), a ~$1.1B/year dividend, and an aggressive new $6B buyback authorization — all depend on gold prices remaining elevated; a sustained price pullback would force difficult trade-offs among these priorities

Consistent insider selling (CEO and multiple EVPs sold shares through September 2026 with no reported insider buying in the trailing three months) and a high reliance on record gold prices rather than volume/production growth to drive recent earnings beats raise questions about the sustainability of current valuation multiples if gold normalizes
